lines.text: A tiny land in the Alps, bought by a family of princes, that became one of the richest countries on Earth. This is the story of Liechtenstein.
It begins with a noble family, first heard of in the eleven hundreds, the House of Liechtenstein, who would give the country its name.
Below its castle on the Rhine grew Vaduz, the town that would become the capital.
The princes bought the lordships of Vaduz and Schellenberg, and in 1719 the emperor made them one principality.
In 1806, when Napoleon gathered German states into his Confederation of the Rhine, Liechtenstein came out of it a sovereign state.
Prince Franz Joseph the second, who reigned from 1938, was the first of his line to actually live in the country.
Having given up its army in 1868, Liechtenstein tied itself to Switzerland in 1923, and uses the Swiss franc to this day.
In 1941 Hilti was founded in Schaan. Its building tools are now used on construction sites around the world.
Hans-Adam the second followed his father in 1989, and still reigns over the principality.
And only in 1984, in a referendum, did the women of Liechtenstein at last win the right to vote.
Small, neutral and prosperous, Liechtenstein keeps its own quiet place in the Alps.
